claim: The study analyzed genomic profiles of 17,879 tumors from patients with known outcomes.
source: To improve our understanding of the molecular alterations that underlie deadly malignancies, we analyzed the genomic profiles of 17,879 tumors from patients with known outcomes.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as the total number of tumors analyzed in the study.

claim: Mutations in almost all cancer driver genes contain remarkably little information on patient prognosis.
source: We find that mutations in almost all cancer driver genes contain remarkably little information on patient prognosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: CNAs in cancer driver genes harbor significant prognostic power.
source: However, CNAs in these same driver genes harbor significant prognostic power.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Focal CNAs are associated with worse outcomes than broad alterations.
source: Focal CNAs are associated with worse outcomes than broad alterations, and CNAs in many driver genes remain prognostic when controlling for stage, grade, TP53 status, and total aneuploidy.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: CNAs in many driver genes remain prognostic when controlling for stage, grade, TP53 status, and total aneuploidy.
source: Focal CNAs are associated with worse outcomes than broad alterations, and CNAs in many driver genes remain prognostic when controlling for stage, grade, TP53 status, and total aneuploidy.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by multivariate analysis data.

claim: A subset of prognostic alterations also confer specific therapeutic vulnerabilities.
source: By performing a meta-analysis across independent patient cohorts, we identify robust prognostic biomarkers in specific cancer types, and we demonstrate that a subset of these alterations also confer specific therapeutic vulnerabilities.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Among individuals diagnosed with early-stage colorectal cancer, about 60% of patients will be cured by surgery alone, while the remaining 40% will experience a recurrence that is frequently fatal.
source: For instance, among individuals diagnosed with early-stage colorectal cancer, about 60% of patients will be cured by surgery alone, while the remaining 40% will experience a recurrence that is frequently fatal (Mäkelä et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mäkelä et al., 1995.

claim: Predictive biomarkers identify patients who are likely to respond to specific therapies.
source: In general, these biomarkers are divided into two classes: predictive and prognostic (Nalejska et al., 2014). Predictive biomarkers identify patients who are likely to respond to specific therapies, like the EGFR mutations that sensitize lung tumors to EGFR inhibition (Paez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to Nalejska et al., 2014 and Paez et al., 2004.

claim: EGFR mutations sensitize lung tumors to EGFR inhibition.
source: Predictive biomarkers identify patients who are likely to respond to specific therapies, like the EGFR mutations that sensitize lung tumors to EGFR inhibition (Paez et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Paez et al., 2004.

claim: Prognostic biomarkers provide information on cancer aggressiveness and the likelihood of patient death.
source: In contrast, prognostic biomarkers provide information on cancer aggressiveness and the likelihood of patient death.
evidence: This is a definition that represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Tumor de-differentiation and lymph-node infiltration serve as prototypical prognostic biomarkers due to their strong association with poor outcomes.
source: Tumor de-differentiation and lymph-node infiltration serve as prototypical prognostic biomarkers due to their strong association with poor outcomes (Connolly et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Connolly et al., 2003.

claim: Pathology-based biomarkers can suffer from low levels of inter-observer concordance.
source: Yet, these pathology-based biomarkers can suffer from low levels of inter-observer concordance (Allsbrook et al., 2001; Coons et al., 1997; Elmore et al., 2015; Gilks et al., 2013), and even perfect pathological assessment yields incomplete information on a patient's most likely clinical course (Bijker et al., 2013; Nofech-Mozes et al., 2005; Young, 2003; Zaniboni et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Even perfect pathological assessment yields incomplete information on a patient's most likely clinical course.
source: Yet, these pathology-based biomarkers can suffer from low levels of inter-observer concordance (Allsbrook et al., 2001; Coons et al., 1997; Elmore et al., 2015; Gilks et al., 2013), and even perfect pathological assessment yields incomplete information on a patient's most likely clinical course (Bijker et al., 2013; Nofech-Mozes et al., 2005; Young, 2003; Zaniboni et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: New methods to identify aggressive tumors could lead to improvements in the stratification of patient risk, better clinical management, and a decrease in dangerous and unnecessary over-treatment.
source: New methods to identify aggressive tumors could lead to improvements in the stratification of patient risk, better clinical management, and a decrease in dangerous and unnecessary over-treatment (Esserman et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Esserman et al., 2013.

claim: The cost of DNA sequencing continues to drop.
source: As the cost of DNA sequencing continues to drop, it has become increasingly feasible for hospitals to implement routine targeted and/or genome-wide analyses of patient tumors (Gagan and Van Allen, 2015; Sholl et al., 2016; Zehir et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: It has become increasingly feasible for hospitals to implement routine targeted and/or genome-wide analyses of patient tumors.
source: As the cost of DNA sequencing continues to drop, it has become increasingly feasible for hospitals to implement routine targeted and/or genome-wide analyses of patient tumors (Gagan and Van Allen, 2015; Sholl et al., 2016; Zehir et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Several DNA-based, therapy-specific predictive biomarkers have been discovered.
source: But, while several DNA-based, therapy-specific predictive biomarkers have been discovered, the prognostic information contained within tumor genomes is much less clear.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: The prognostic information contained within tumor genomes is much less clear.
source: But, while several DNA-based, therapy-specific predictive biomarkers have been discovered, the prognostic information contained within tumor genomes is much less clear.
evidence: This is a statement that sets up the rationale for the study.

claim: Previous genome-wide efforts to discover novel prognostic biomarkers have largely focused on the gene expression changes associated with patient mortality.
source: Previous genome-wide efforts to discover novel prognostic biomarkers have largely focused on the gene expression changes associated with patient mortality (Anaya, 2016; Anaya et al., 2015; Gentles et al., 2015; Uhlen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Gene expression studies have identified a set of transcripts that encode proteins involved in cell cycle progression that correlate with recurrence and death in several cancer types.
source: These studies have identified a set of transcripts that encode proteins involved in cell cycle progression that correlate with recurrence and death in several cancer types (Cuzick et al., 2011; Dancik and Theodorescu, 2015; Gentles et al., 2015; Mosley and Keri, 2008; Venet et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2012; Wistuba et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Comparatively less is known about how changes at the DNA level affect patient survival.
source: Comparatively less is known about how changes at the DNA level affect patient survival.
evidence: This is a statement that sets up the rationale for the study.

claim: Reports in the literature commonly suggest that mutations in driver oncogenes are associated with poor outcomes, including KRAS mutations in lung cancer, PIK3CA mutations in breast cancer, and BRAF mutations in colorectal cancer.
source: Reports in the literature commonly suggest that mutations in driver oncogenes are associated with poor outcomes, including, for instance, KRAS mutations in lung cancer (Guan et al., 2013; Marabese et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2013), PIK3CA mutations in breast cancer (Li et al., 2006; Oshiro et al., 2015), and BRAF mutations in colorectal cancer (Richman et al., 2009; Roth et al., 2010; Tol et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Other studies of the same genes in the same cancer types have failed to observe any significant associations with outcome.
source: Other studies of the same genes in the same cancer types have failed to observe any significant associations with outcome (Bozhanov et al., 2010; Gonzalez-Angulo et al., 2009; Hutchins et al., 2011; Pang et al., 2014; Scoccianti et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutation-based biomarker studies may be confounded by small samples sizes, post-hoc hypothesis testing, imprecise clinical endpoints, and the 'file drawer' problem.
source: In general, mutation-based biomarker studies may be confounded by small samples sizes, post-hoc hypothesis testing, imprecise clinical endpoints, and the so-called 'file drawer' problem, in which negative findings are less likely to be published (Aronson, 2005; Ensor, 2014; Goossens et al., 2015; Rosenthal, 1979; Scargle, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The prognostic information captured by sequencing driver oncogenes remains unknown.
source: The prognostic information captured by sequencing driver oncogenes remains unknown, and a pan-cancer, exome-wide analysis of outcome-associated mutations has not been conducted.
evidence: This is a statement that sets up the rationale for the study.

claim: A pan-cancer, exome-wide analysis of outcome-associated mutations has not been conducted.
source: The prognostic information captured by sequencing driver oncogenes remains unknown, and a pan-cancer, exome-wide analysis of outcome-associated mutations has not been conducted.
evidence: This is a statement that sets up the rationale for the study.

claim: Highly-aneuploid tumors tend to have worse outcomes than diploid tumors.
source: Previous investigations into the prognostic importance of DNA copy number alterations (CNAs) have indicated that highly-aneuploid tumors tend to have worse outcomes than diploid tumors (Friedlander et al., 1984; Kallioniemi et al., 1987; Kokal et al., 1986; Merkel and McGuire, 1990; Zimmerman et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Previous CNA analyses have largely focused either on arm-length changes or on alterations that affect single oncogenes or tumor suppressors.
source: However, these analyses have largely focused either on arm-length changes (Davoli et al., 2017; Roy et al., 2016) or on alterations that affect single oncogenes or tumor suppressors (Deming et al., 2000; Shi et al., 2012; Srividya et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The functional importance of copy number changes in most genes at the single-gene level is unknown.
source: The functional importance of copy number changes in most genes at the single-gene level is unknown, and a pan-cancer, gene-by-gene analysis of prognostic copy number alterations has not been conducted.
evidence: This is a statement that sets up the rationale for the study.

claim: A pan-cancer, gene-by-gene analysis of prognostic copy number alterations has not been conducted.
source: The functional importance of copy number changes in most genes at the single-gene level is unknown, and a pan-cancer, gene-by-gene analysis of prognostic copy number alterations has not been conducted.
evidence: This is a statement that sets up the rationale for the study.

claim: The study collected and analyzed molecular profiles from a 'discovery' set of 9442 patients and a 'validation' set of 8618 patients with solid tumors.
source: In order to gain a global understanding of the genomic features in a primary tumor that influence cancer prognosis, we collected and analyzed molecular profiles from a 'discovery' set of 9442 patients and a 'validation' set of 8618 patients with solid tumors.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as the study design.

claim: The study provides a web portal to facilitate community access to the biomarker dataset at http://survival.cshl.edu.
source: Additionally, we provide a web portal to facilitate community access to this rich biomarker dataset at http://survival.cshl.edu.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction.

claim: The study analyzed multiple classes of genomic data from 9442 patients with 16 types of cancer from the TCGA.
source: To determine the differences between benign and fatal tumors, we first analyzed multiple classes of genomic data from 9442 patients with 16 types of cancer from the TCGA (outlined in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; abbreviations are defined in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section.

claim: Cox univariate proportional hazards models were generated linking the presence or expression of a particular feature with clinical outcome.
source: For every tumor type and every dataset, we generated Cox univariate proportional hazards models linking the presence or expression of a particular feature with clinical outcome (described in Supplemental Text 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section as the analytical method used.

claim: If the presence of a mutation or copy number amplification is significantly associated with patient death, then a Z score >1.96 corresponds to a P value < 0.05.
source: If the presence of a mutation or copy number amplification is significantly associated with patient death, then a Z score >1.96 corresponds to a P value < 0.05 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: A Z score less than −1.96 indicates that the presence of a mutation is associated with survival or that a gene deletion is significantly associated with patient death.
source: In contrast, a Z score less than −1.96 indicates that the presence of a mutation is associated with survival or that a gene deletion is significantly associated with patient death.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section as the interpretation of Z scores.

claim: Significant differences in clinical outcome were observed according to a cancer's tissue-of-origin.
source: As expected, we observed significant differences in clinical outcome according to a cancer's tissue-of-origin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Prostate cancer had the least aggressive clinical course, with a median survival time that was not reached in this dataset (>4600 days).
source: Prostate cancer had the least aggressive clinical course, with a median survival time that was not reached in this dataset (>4600 days), while pancreatic cancer conferred the worst prognosis (median survival time: 444 days).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section.

claim: Pancreatic cancer conferred the worst prognosis with a median survival time of 444 days.
source: Prostate cancer had the least aggressive clinical course, with a median survival time that was not reached in this dataset (>4600 days), while pancreatic cancer conferred the worst prognosis (median survival time: 444 days).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section.

claim: The 5 year survival frequencies of patients in the TCGA were highly similar to the national averages reported by NCI-SEER (R = 0.83, p < 0.0001).
source: Overall, the 5 year survival frequencies of patients in the TCGA were highly similar to the national averages reported by NCI-SEER (R = 0.83, p < 0.0001), suggesting that the patients included in this analysis are broadly representative of the general population (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The patients included in the TCGA analysis are broadly representative of the general population.
source: Overall, the 5 year survival frequencies of patients in the TCGA were highly similar to the national averages reported by NCI-SEER (R = 0.83, p < 0.0001), suggesting that the patients included in this analysis are broadly representative of the general population (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison with NCI-SEER data.

claim: The analysis of inferred patient sex exhibited >99% concordance with patients' self-reported sex.
source: Next, we inferred patient sex on the basis of chromosome-specific gene expression patterns (Gentles et al., 2015; van den Berge and Sijen, 2017). Our analysis exhibited >99% concordance with patients' self-reported sex, further verifying the overall accuracy of the clinical annotations and our data processing pipeline (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Among the 30 most-frequently mutated cancer driver genes, only two (EGFR and TP53) were associated with prognosis in more than two tumor types.
source: We first focused on known oncogenes and tumor suppressors, and found that among the 30 most-frequently mutated cancer driver genes, only two (EGFR and TP53) were associated with prognosis in more than two tumor types (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: TP53 mutations were linked to outcome in five of 16 cancer types.
source: TP53 mutations were linked to outcome in five of 16 cancer types, though the differences in patient survival were generally small (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B.

claim: The differences in patient survival associated with TP53 mutations were generally small.
source: TP53 mutations were linked to outcome in five of 16 cancer types, though the differences in patient survival were generally small (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B.

claim: Mutations in KRAS, PIK3CA, CDKN2A, BRAF, KMT2D, ATM, SMAD4, and many other genes were frequently observed but were never significantly linked with patient outcome.
source: In contrast, many other cancer driver genes were not associated with survival time in any tumor type. While mutations in KRAS, PIK3CA, CDKN2A, BRAF, KMT2D, ATM, SMAD4, and many other genes were frequently observed, they were never significantly linked with patient outcome (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: IDH1c132 mutations were significantly associated with a favorable prognosis in glioma.
source: IDH1c132 mutations were significantly associated with a favorable prognosis in glioma, but other recurrently-mutated codons (KRASc12, PIK3CAc1047, TP53c273, etc.) were largely uninformative (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D.

claim: Other recurrently-mutated codons (KRASc12, PIK3CAc1047, TP53c273, etc.) were largely uninformative.
source: IDH1c132 mutations were significantly associated with a favorable prognosis in glioma, but other recurrently-mutated codons (KRASc12, PIK3CAc1047, TP53c273, etc.) were largely uninformative (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D.

claim: Considering only 'hotspot' mutations in each gene failed to uncover robust survival associations.
source: Then, we identified 'hotspot' residues that were mutated in at least five different patients across all cohorts. Considering only these 'hotspot' mutations in each gene also failed to uncover robust survival associations (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4E.

claim: Cancer type-specific recurrent mutations (FGFR3c249 in BLCA, CTNNB1c37 in UCEC, etc.) were uninformative.
source: Finally, we identified cancer type-specific recurrent mutations, but these alterations (FGFR3c249 in BLCA, CTNNB1c37 in UCEC, etc.) were similarly uninformative (Figure 1—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4F.

claim: Very few patients were treated with BRAF or EGFR inhibitors.
source: However, due to the time-frame of sample collection, very few patients were treated with BRAF or EGFR inhibitors, and removing those patients who had received these therapies failed to significantly affect Z scores (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Removing patients who had received BRAF or EGFR inhibitors failed to significantly affect Z scores.
source: However, due to the time-frame of sample collection, very few patients were treated with BRAF or EGFR inhibitors, and removing those patients who had received these therapies failed to significantly affect Z scores (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Excluding patients with hyper-mutated tumors had minimal effect on the prognostic significance of driver gene mutations.
source: Hyper-mutation within a subset of cancers could increase mutational 'noise' and decrease our ability to identify prognostic signatures, but excluding patients with hyper-mutated tumors had minimal effect on the prognostic significance of driver gene mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B and Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 5B and Supplementary file 2C.

claim: Patients harboring mutations in two cancer driver genes that were not prognostic alone had the same risk of death as patients with wild-type copies of one or both genes.
source: We found that, in general, patients harboring mutations in two cancer driver genes that were not prognostic alone had the same risk of death as patients with wild-type copies of one or both genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 5C.

claim: Restricting analysis to mutations with high VAFs failed to identify more prognostic genes.
source: We found that restricting our analysis to mutations with high VAFs failed to identify more prognostic genes, indicating that patient stratification is unlikely to be improved by assessing only clonal mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Patient stratification is unlikely to be improved by assessing only clonal mutations.
source: We found that restricting our analysis to mutations with high VAFs failed to identify more prognostic genes, indicating that patient stratification is unlikely to be improved by assessing only clonal mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the VAF analysis.

claim: Cancer driver gene mutations lacked significant patient stratification power.
source: These analyses suggested that, in general, cancer driver gene mutations lacked significant patient stratification power.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the preceding analyses.

claim: In breast cancer and lung adenocarcinoma, 128 and 3996 genes were mutated in ≥2% of patients, respectively, but none of these mutations were significantly correlated with patient outcome at a 5% FDR.
source: For instance, in breast cancer and lung adenocarcinoma, 128 and 3996 genes were mutated in ≥2% of patients, respectively, but none of these mutations were significantly correlated with patient outcome at a 5% FDR.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section.

claim: Most mutations in cancer genomes lack significant prognostic power.
source: In total, these results indicate that most mutations in cancer genomes lack significant prognostic power.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the preceding analyses.

claim: The five genes with the strongest survival associations were all observed in the GBMLGG (pan-glioma) cohort.
source: In our above analysis, we noted that the five genes with the strongest survival associations were all observed in the GBMLGG (pan-glioma) cohort.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section.

claim: PTEN and EGFR mutations conferred dismal prognosis in glioma.
source: Among the top-scoring genes, we found that PTEN and EGFR mutations conferred dismal prognosis, while mutations in IDH1, TP53, and ATRX were associated with favorable prognosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 7A.

claim: Mutations in IDH1, TP53, and ATRX were associated with favorable prognosis in glioma.
source: Among the top-scoring genes, we found that PTEN and EGFR mutations conferred dismal prognosis, while mutations in IDH1, TP53, and ATRX were associated with favorable prognosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 7A.

claim: Mutations in IDH1, TP53, and ATRX were most frequently observed in low-grade gliomas.
source: Mutations in these genes have previously been linked to distinct glioma subtypes (Ceccarelli et al., 2016; Kannan et al., 2012; Suzuki et al., 2015), and we verified that mutations in IDH1, TP53, and ATRX were most frequently observed in low-grade gliomas, while mutations in PTEN and EGFR were most frequently observed in high-grade glioblastomas (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 7B and citations.

claim: Mutations in PTEN and EGFR were most frequently observed in high-grade glioblastomas.
source: Mutations in these genes have previously been linked to distinct glioma subtypes (Ceccarelli et al., 2016; Kannan et al., 2012; Suzuki et al., 2015), and we verified that mutations in IDH1, TP53, and ATRX were most frequently observed in low-grade gliomas, while mutations in PTEN and EGFR were most frequently observed in high-grade glioblastomas (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 7B and citations.

claim: IDH1 mutations were independently associated with prolonged survival in both low-grade gliomas and high-grade glioblastomas.
source: For instance, while IDH1 mutations were more common in low-grade gliomas, they were occasionally observed in high-grade tumors as well, and they were independently associated with prolonged survival in both cohorts (Figure 1—figure supplement 7C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 7C.

claim: EGFR mutations were associated with poor outcomes in low-grade gliomas but were non-prognostic in high-grade glioblastomas.
source: In contrast, when EGFR mutations were observed in low-grade gliomas, they were associated poor outcomes, but EGFR mutations were non-prognostic in high-grade glioblastomas (Figure 1—figure supplement 7D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 7D.

claim: In gliomas, mutations contain both subtype-dependent and subtype-independent prognostic information.
source: Thus, in gliomas, mutations contain both subtype-dependent and subtype-independent prognostic information.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the preceding glioma analyses.

claim: Outside of glioma and the tumor suppressor TP53, mutations in most cancer driver genes are non-prognostic.
source: However, outside of this cancer type and the tumor suppressor TP53, mutations in most cancer driver genes are non-prognostic.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the preceding analyses.

claim: The copy number of oncogenes and tumor suppressors was frequently linked with patient outcome.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the copy number of these oncogenes and tumor suppressors was frequently linked with patient outcome (Figure 2 and Supplementary file 3A-B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2 and Supplementary file 3A-B.

claim: Amplification of EGFR, PIK3CA, and BRAF, and deletion of CDKN2A, RB1 and EP300 were strongly associated with shorter patient survival times in four or more cancer types each.
source: Amplification of EGFR, PIK3CA, and BRAF, and deletion of CDKN2A, RB1 and EP300 were strongly associated with shorter patient survival times in four or more cancer types each.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section.

claim: While mutations in PIK3CA were never informative, the copy number of PIK3CA was associated with outcome in breast, colorectal, glioma, lung-squamous, pancreas, and prostate cancers.
source: Copy number was prognostic even for genes in which mutations were not linked with outcome: for instance, while mutations in PIK3CA were never informative, the copy number of PIK3CA was associated with outcome in breast, colorectal, glioma, lung-squamous, pancreas, and prostate cancers (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2B and D.

claim: Among the 30 most frequently-mutated cancer driver genes, 108 significant associations were detected between gene copy number and outcome, compared to 23 associations between mutation and outcome.
source: Overall, among the 30 most frequently-mutated cancer driver genes, we detected 108 significant associations between gene copy number and outcome, compared to 23 associations between mutation and outcome.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section.

claim: For 28 out of 30 driver genes, DNA copy number was prognostic in more cancer types than mutational status was.
source: For 28 out of 30 driver genes, DNA copy number was prognostic in more cancer types than mutational status was.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section.

claim: Determining the copy number of oncogenes and tumor suppressors in a primary tumor can better stratify patient risk than assessing single base-pair mutations.
source: We conclude that determining the copy number of oncogenes and tumor suppressors in a primary tumor can better stratify patient risk than assessing single base-pair mutations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the preceding CNA analyses.

claim: Trichotomizing CNA values into 'deletions', 'amplifications', and 'copy-neutral' resulted in 94 significant survival associations.
source: To test this possibility, we trichotomized CNA values into 'deletions' (<−0.3), 'amplifications' (>0.3), and 'copy-neutral' (≥−0.3 and≤0.3). We then calculated Cox regressions at the same 30 loci using the discretized copy number values. This analysis resulted in 94 significant survival associations, more than four times as many significant features as when mutations were analyzed, and comparable to the number of significant features that resulted using continuous CNA values (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The greater prognostic significance of CNAs is not simply a consequence of the continuous nature of copy number data.
source: This analysis suggests that the greater prognostic significance of CNAs is not simply a consequence of the continuous nature of copy number data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the trichotomization analysis.

claim: The most significant survival-associated copy number changes genome-wide were found on chromosome 9p in a valley that precisely included the tumor suppressor CDKN2A.
source: The most significant survival-associated copy number changes genome-wide were found on chromosome 9p in a valley that precisely included the tumor suppressor CDKN2A.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section.

claim: Z score peaks were found at loci that include oncogenes PIK3CA, EGFR, MYC, CCNE1, and others.
source: Z score peaks were found at loci that include oncogenes PIK3CA, EGFR, MYC, CCNE1, and others.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section.

claim: The overlap of Z score peaks with known driver genes suggests that the copy number of these oncogenes and tumor suppressors directly influence the risk of cancer patient death.
source: This overlap suggests that, in many instances, the copy number of these oncogenes and tumor suppressors directly influence the risk of cancer patient death.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overlap of Z score peaks with known driver genes.

claim: Sample purity was inconsistently-associated with patient outcome.
source: We found that sample purity was inconsistently-associated with patient outcome (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Higher tumor purity determined by either pathological analysis or ABSOLUTE was associated with worse outcome in only one of 16 cohorts, each.
source: For instance, higher tumor purity determined by either pathological analysis or ABSOLUTE was associated with worse outcome in only one of 16 cohorts, each (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: The lack of a strong correlation between infiltrating cell populations and clinical prognosis suggests that analyte purity is insufficient to explain the relationship between CNAs and patient survival.
source: The lack of a strong correlation between infiltrating cell populations and clinical prognosis suggests that analyte purity is insufficient to explain the relationship between CNAs and patient survival.
evidence: This is an inference based on the purity analysis.

claim: Driver gene CNAs remain broadly prognostic in multivariate models that include gene copy number and tumor purity measurements.
source: Secondly, we generated multivariate Cox models that included gene copy number and these three measurements of tumor purity, and we found that driver gene CNAs remain broadly prognostic in these bivariate models (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and Supplementary file 3C-E).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and Supplementary file 3C-E.

claim: Amplification of Cyclin E1 is associated with poor prognosis in ovarian cancer, even when analysis was restricted to high-purity tumor samples and samples that lacked significant leukocyte presence.
source: For instance, we discovered that amplification of Cyclin E1 is associated with poor prognosis in ovarian cancer, and this remained true even when our analysis was restricted to high-purity tumor samples and samples that lacked significant leukocyte presence (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The interrelationship between aneuploidy and immunological tolerance likely plays an important role in tumor development, but it is not the primary driver of CNA-associated patient mortality.
source: Thus, while the interrelationship between aneuploidy and immunological tolerance likely plays an important role in tumor development, this analysis suggests that it is not the primary driver of CNA-associated patient mortality.
evidence: This is an inference based on the purity analysis.

claim: Z scores generated from either univariate models or multivariate models that included stage or grade were highly correlated (R = 0.91 and R = 0.96 respectively).
source: We found that Z scores generated from either univariate models or multivariate models that included stage or grade were highly correlated (R = 0.91 and R = 0.96 respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and Supplementary file 4.

claim: 71% of prognostic CNAs in individual cancer types remained prognostic in multivariate models that included stage or grade.
source: Overall, 71% of prognostic CNAs in individual cancer types remained prognostic in these multivariate models (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Including gene-level copy-number assessment can significantly improve the stratification of patient risk beyond standard clinical parameters.
source: Thus, including gene-level copy-number assessment can significantly improve the stratification of patient risk beyond standard clinical parameters (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–D.

claim: Gene-level copy number values remained prognostic when separating TCGA cohorts by cancer subtype.
source: Gene-level copy number values also remained prognostic when separating TCGA cohorts by cancer subtype (Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Supplementary file 4F-G).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Supplementary file 4F-G.

claim: CNA Z scores values were highly correlated between the bulk GBMLGG cohort and the individual GBM and LGG subtypes (R = 0.68 and R = 0.86, respectively).
source: For instance, CNA Z scores values were highly correlated between the bulk GBMLGG cohort and the individual GBM and LGG subtypes (R = 0.68 and R = 0.86, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: EGFR amplifications remained associated with outcome in both the LGG and GBM cohorts.
source: While analyzing the GBM cohort separately abolished the prognostic significance of EGFR mutations (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D), EGFR amplifications remained associated with outcome in both the LGG and GBM cohorts (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B–C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4B–C.

claim: Amplifications in MYC and PIK3CA were prognostic in multiple tumor subtypes.
source: Amplifications in MYC and PIK3CA were similarly prognostic in multiple tumor subtypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D–E and Supplementary file 4G).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4D–E and Supplementary file 4G.

claim: CDKN2A deletion is a strong indicator of poor prognosis in the pan-kidney cohort, in clear cell carcinomas, and in papillary cell carcinomas, but did not reach statistical significance when kidney chromophobe carcinomas were analyzed independently.
source: CDKN2A deletion is a strong indicator of poor prognosis in the pan-kidney cohort, in clear cell carcinomas, and in papillary cell carcinomas, but did not reach statistical significance when kidney chromophobe carcinomas were analyzed independently (Figure 2—figure supplement 4F–G).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4F–G.

claim: Larger cohort numbers may be needed to identify the strongest biomarkers in rare cancer subtypes.
source: At other loci, low patient numbers from certain subtypes may obscure the detection of specific biomarkers. For instance, within the KIPAN cohort, 67% of tumors are clear cell carcinomas, 23% of tumors are papillary cell carcinomas, and 10% of tumors are chromophobe carcinomas. CDKN2A deletion is a strong indicator of poor prognosis in the pan-kidney cohort, in clear cell carcinomas, and in papillary cell carcinomas, but did not reach statistical significance when kidney chromophobe carcinomas were analyzed independently (Figure 2—figure supplement 4F–G). In total, these results underscore the ability of driver gene CNAs to improve patient stratification when controlling for tumor identity, though larger cohort numbers may be needed to identify the strongest biomarkers in rare cancer subtypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the subtype analysis.

claim: TP53-mutant tumors exhibit more aneuploidy than TP53-wild-type tumors.
source: Using an 'aneuploidy score' for each tumor based on the total number of arm-length alterations (Taylor et al., 2018), we verified that TP53-mutant tumors exhibit more aneuploidy than TP53-wild-type tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and that total aneuploidy is a poor prognosis factor in several cancer types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Total aneuploidy is a poor prognosis factor in several cancer types.
source: Using an 'aneuploidy score' for each tumor based on the total number of arm-length alterations (Taylor et al., 2018), we verified that TP53-mutant tumors exhibit more aneuploidy than TP53-wild-type tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and that total aneuploidy is a poor prognosis factor in several cancer types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In multivariate models that included TP53 mutation status, 33 of 40 (83%) gene-level CNAs remained prognostic.
source: In multivariate models that included TP53 mutation status, 33 of 40 (83%) gene-level CNAs remained prognostic, demonstrating that these CNAs are not linked with death due to an indirect association with TP53 status (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: Gene-level CNAs are not linked with death due to an indirect association with TP53 status.
source: In multivariate models that included TP53 mutation status, 33 of 40 (83%) gene-level CNAs remained prognostic, demonstrating that these CNAs are not linked with death due to an indirect association with TP53 status (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the multivariate analysis.

claim: In multivariate models that included total tumor aneuploidy, 80% of gene-level CNAs were still associated with outcome.
source: Similarly, in multivariate models that included total tumor aneuploidy, 80% of these CNAs were still associated with outcome (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D.

claim: The total structural alteration burden was associated with outcome in multiple tumor types.
source: Finally, as a proxy for the total structural alteration burden, we summed the number of breakpoints (as indicated by discrete copy number values along a chromosome) in each tumor (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). This metric was associated with outcome in multiple tumor types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), but 75% of driver gene CNAs remained prognostic in multivariate models that included this score (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 75% of driver gene CNAs remained prognostic in multivariate models that included the total structural alteration burden.
source: Finally, as a proxy for the total structural alteration burden, we summed the number of breakpoints (as indicated by discrete copy number values along a chromosome) in each tumor (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). This metric was associated with outcome in multiple tumor types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), but 75% of driver gene CNAs remained prognostic in multivariate models that included this score (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–F.

claim: Assessing gene-level tumor CNAs can yield more prognostic information than simply screening for TP53 mutations or measuring bulk levels of tumor aneuploidy.
source: These results indicate that assessing gene-level tumor CNAs can yield more prognostic information than simply screening for TP53 mutations or measuring bulk levels of tumor aneuploidy (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the multivariate analyses.

claim: Broad CNAs were associated with moderately worse outcomes, while focal CNAs were associated with sharp declines in survival.
source: Among loci at which both broad and focal alterations were observed, we frequently found that broad CNAs were associated with moderately worse outcomes, while focal CNAs were associated with sharp declines in survival (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3A–B.

claim: At some loci, broad CNAs had outcomes that were indistinguishable from copy-neutral tumors, while only focal CNAs were associated with death.
source: At some loci, broad CNAs had outcomes that were indistinguishable from copy-neutral tumors, while only focal CNAs were associated with death (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: Instances in which broad CNAs indicated a worse prognosis than a focal alteration were rarely detected.
source: We rarely detected instances in which broad CNAs indicated a worse prognosis than a focal alteration (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3A.

claim: Large copy number alterations change the dosage of multiple genes at once and can impair tumor growth, while targeted alterations that specifically affect driver gene copy number maximize malignant potential.
source: We interpret these results as a reflection of aneuploidy-induced fitness penalties (Sheltzer et al., 2017; Sheltzer and Amon, 2011): large copy number alterations change the dosage of multiple genes at once and can impair tumor growth, while targeted alterations that specifically affect driver gene copy number maximize malignant potential.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the focal vs. broad CNA analysis and supported by citations.

claim: A significant correlation was found between transcript levels and gene copy number changes at 98% of the analyzed prognostic genes.
source: To test the effects of prognostic CNAs on gene expression, we compared transcript levels and gene copy number changes at 40 prognostic loci and found a significant correlation between the two at 98% of the analyzed genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: At 95% of test loci, gene copy number remained prognostic in multivariate models that also included gene mutation status.
source: Interestingly, this is not the case: at 95% of our test loci, gene copy number remained prognostic in multivariate models that also included gene mutation status (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3D.

claim: In colorectal cancer, amplification of EGFR was associated with death even in tumors that lacked EGFR mutations.
source: For instance, in colorectal cancer, amplification of EGFR was associated with death even in tumors that lacked EGFR mutations (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 3E.

claim: Even at recurrently-mutated loci, changes in the expression of the wild-type gene can have a profound effect on cancer cell behavior.
source: In total, these results indicate that even at recurrently-mutated loci, changes in the expression of the wild-type gene can have a profound effect on cancer cell behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of CNAs and mutations.

claim: The mutation frequencies and the Z scores of recurrent mutations were highly similar between the ICGC and TCGA cohorts (R = 0.67, p < 0.0001, and R = 0.56, p < 0.0001, respectively).
source: Overall, the mutation frequencies and the Z scores of recurrent mutations were highly similar between the ICGC and TCGA cohorts (R = 0.67, p < 0.0001, and R = 0.56, p < 0.0001, respectively; Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 4A–B.

claim: Consistent with the TCGA analysis, mutations in TP53 were associated with outcome in more patient cohorts than any other gene in the ICGC dataset.
source: Consistent with our TCGA analysis, mutations in TP53 were associated with outcome in more patient cohorts than any other gene (Figure 4C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 4C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–D.

claim: Other mutations, including in known cancer driver genes, were rarely associated with outcome in individual cancer types and harbored minimal pan-cancer significance in the ICGC dataset.
source: Other mutations, including in known cancer driver genes, were rarely associated with outcome in individual cancer types and harbored minimal pan-cancer significance (Figure 4D–F and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 4D–F and Supplementary file 6.

claim: Mutations in KRAS, PIK3CA, BRAF, APC, PTEN, CDKN2A, and many others were frequently observed but were never correlated with outcome in the ICGC dataset.
source: Mutations in KRAS, PIK3CA, BRAF, APC, PTEN, CDKN2A, and many others were frequently observed but were never correlated with outcome (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 4D.

claim: Numerous amplifications and deletions were found to be associated with patient mortality in 2431 additional patients with CNA data curated by cBioportal.
source: We next analyzed 2431 additional patients with CNA data curated by cBioportal, and found numerous amplifications and deletions associated with patient mortality (Supplementary file 6C).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Supplementary file 6C.

claim: In breast cancer, prognostic amplifications were found centered around oncogenes, including ERBB2, MYC, and MDM2, while prognostic deletions encompassed tumor suppressors CDKN2A, PTEN, and TP53.
source: In breast cancer, we found prognostic amplifications that were centered around oncogenes, including ERBB2, MYC, and MDM2, while prognostic deletions encompassed tumor suppressors CDKN2A, PTEN, and TP53 (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 4G.

claim: A highly significant correlation was observed between the meta-Z scores obtained from the TCGA and cBioportal datasets (R = 0.42).
source: Overall, we observed a highly significant correlation between the meta-Z scores obtained from the TCGA and cBioportal datasets (R = 0.42; Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 4H.

claim: In patient cohorts subjected to both mutation and copy number analysis, CNAs in driver genes commonly harbored greater prognostic significance than mutations in those same genes.
source: Finally, in patient cohorts subjected to both mutation and copy number analysis, we verified that CNAs in driver genes commonly harbored greater prognostic significance than mutations in those same genes (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 4I.

claim: In breast cancer, among 25 frequently-mutated genes, mutations in only two genes (TP53 and GATA3) displayed prognostic significance, while CNAs in 12 of those same genes were associated with patient outcome.
source: For instance, in breast cancer, among 25 frequently-mutated genes, mutations in only two genes (TP53 and GATA3) displayed prognostic significance, while CNAs in 12 of those same genes were associated with patient outcome (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 4J.

claim: The survival patterns discovered in the TCGA dataset are conserved across independent cohorts of cancer patients.
source: In total, these analyses suggest that the survival patterns discovered in the TCGA dataset are conserved across independent cohorts of cancer patients.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the validation analyses.

claim: While mutations in most cancer driver genes are non-prognostic, copy number alterations in these same genes are tightly linked with patient outcome.
source: In particular, while mutations in most cancer driver genes are non-prognostic, copy number alterations in these same genes are tightly linked with patient outcome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the validation analyses.

claim: The combined patient dataset included two to six independent cohorts from each of 13 common cancer types, comprising 16,580 total patients.
source: Our combined patient dataset therefore included two to six independent cohorts from each of 13 common cancer types, comprising 16,580 total patients.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section.

claim: Alterations that were consistently associated with outcome despite significant differences in cohort collection and analysis would represent highly-penetrant biomarkers of patient prognosis.
source: These cohorts were collected at different locations, in different patient populations, using different study designs, and the samples were analyzed using different genomic technologies. We reasoned that alterations that were consistently associated with outcome despite these significant differences would represent highly-penetrant biomarkers of patient prognosis.
evidence: This is a rationale statement for the cross-cohort analysis.

claim: Multiple high-confidence genetic biomarkers of patient outcome were revealed, including MDM4 amplifications in prostate cancer, NOTCH2 amplifications in melanoma, and 2q32 deletions in ovarian cancer.
source: This approach revealed multiple high-confidence genetic biomarkers of patient outcome that, to our knowledge, were novel, including MDM4 amplifications in prostate cancer, NOTCH2 amplifications in melanoma, and 2q32 deletions in ovarian cancer (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Supplementary file 8.

claim: Top-scoring CNAs remained prognostic in multivariate models that included commonly-measured prognostic criteria (Gleason score in prostate cancer, Hepatitis serology in liver cancer, etc.).
source: These robust biomarkers allowed a striking stratification of patient risk, and top-scoring CNAs remained prognostic in multivariate models that included commonly-measured prognostic criteria (Gleason score in prostate cancer, Hepatitis serology in liver cancer, etc.; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Consistent with single-cohort analyses, cross-cohort prognostic CNAs were significantly more common than prognostic mutations.
source: Consistent with our single-cohort analyses, cross-cohort prognostic CNAs were significantly more common than prognostic mutations, and TP53 was the only gene whose mutation status was associated with outcome in more than one cancer type (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: TP53 was the only gene whose mutation status was associated with outcome in more than one cancer type in the cross-cohort analysis.
source: Consistent with our single-cohort analyses, cross-cohort prognostic CNAs were significantly more common than prognostic mutations, and TP53 was the only gene whose mutation status was associated with outcome in more than one cancer type (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: STAG2-mutant gliomas were exquisitely sensitive to treatment with the PARP inhibitor olaparib.
source: For instance, we identified mutations in STAG2 as a high-confidence biomarker of poor prognosis in glioma, and we found that STAG2-mutant gliomas were exquisitely sensitive to treatment with the PARP inhibitor olaparib (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section and supported by Figure 5A.

claim: Highly-significant therapeutic vulnerabilities were identified for 49% of the prognostic biomarkers uncovered by the integrated analysis.
source: In total, we identified highly-significant therapeutic vulnerabilities for 49% of the prognostic biomarkers uncovered by our integrated analysis, providing potential strategies to treat a subset of patients who have the most aggressive cancers.
evidence: This is stated directly in the results section.

claim: Modern medicine has vastly prolonged the survival of individuals diagnosed with cancer.
source: Modern medicine has vastly prolonged the survival of individuals diagnosed with cancer (Johnson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Johnson et al., 2017.

claim: Increasing evidence suggests that large subsets of patients receive sub-optimal care, and are over-treated or under-treated relative to their level of risk.
source: However, increasing evidence suggests that large subsets of patients receive sub-optimal care, and are over-treated or under-treated relative to their level of risk (Bhatt and Klotz, 2016; Esserman et al., 2013; Swaminathan and Swaminathan, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Many of the genetic alterations that differentiate fatal and benign tumors have remained obscure.
source: To date, many of the genetic alterations that differentiate fatal and benign tumors have remained obscure.
evidence: This is a statement that sets up the rationale for the study.

claim: The analysis of prognostic biomarkers from 17,879 patients sheds light on genetic differences between fatal and benign tumors, identifies a subset of patients who may benefit the most from aggressive intervention, and suggests therapeutic strategies for tumors harboring certain alterations associated with poor prognosis.
source: Our analysis of prognostic biomarkers from 17,879 patients sheds light on these genetic differences, identifies a subset of patients who may benefit the most from aggressive intervention, and suggests therapeutic strategies for tumors harboring certain alterations associated with poor prognosis.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's contributions.

claim: Substantial disagreements exist in the literature on the value of mutation-based prognostic biomarkers.
source: Substantial disagreements exist in the literature on the value of mutation-based prognostic biomarkers, as the same driver oncogenes have been independently reported to be either adverse or non-significant prognostic features (Guan et al., 2013; Marabese et al., 2015; Scoccianti et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The study performed an unbiased genome-wide analysis of public datasets with pre-established sample sizes.
source: In this manuscript, we performed an unbiased genome-wide analysis of public datasets with pre-established sample sizes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the discussion section.

claim: The study's approach may bypass certain problems, including post-hoc hypothesis testing, patient-selection bias, and the 'file-drawer problem', that can confound targeted biomarker studies.
source: This approach may therefore bypass certain problems, including post-hoc hypothesis testing, patient-selection bias, and the 'file-drawer problem', that can confound targeted biomarker studies (Aronson, 2005; Ensor, 2014; Goossens et al., 2015; Rosenthal, 1979; Scargle, 1999).
evidence: This is an inference about the study's approach, supported by citations.

claim: With larger sample sizes or more-specific tumor subtypes, additional prognostic mutations could be identified.
source: We consider it possible that, with larger sample sizes or more-specific tumor subtypes, additional prognostic mutations could be identified.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research.

claim: In most patient cohorts analyzed, tumors were analyzed on multiple genomic platforms, and CNAs were commonly prognostic in the same cohorts in which gene mutations were not.
source: Importantly, in most patient cohorts that we collected, tumors were analyzed on multiple genomic platforms, and CNAs were commonly prognostic in the same cohorts in which gene mutations were not.
evidence: This is stated directly in the discussion section.

claim: In a head-to-head comparison, copy number alterations provide more useful prognostic information than single-gene mutations.
source: These results underscore our ability to successfully detect biomarkers in cohorts of these sizes, and suggest that, in a head-to-head comparison, copy number alterations provide more useful prognostic information than single-gene mutations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: The study revealed a subset of mutations with tissue-specific prognostic power, including TP53 mutations in breast cancer, RB1 mutations in bladder cancer, and FBXW7 mutations in colorectal cancer.
source: First, our analysis revealed a subset of mutations with tissue-specific prognostic power, including TP53 mutations in breast cancer, RB1 mutations in bladder cancer, and FBXW7 mutations in colorectal cancer.
evidence: This is stated directly in the discussion section.

claim: Most patients in the TCGA cohorts were treated with standard cytotoxic drugs.
source: Secondly, most patients in the TCGA cohorts were treated with standard cytotoxic drugs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the discussion section.

claim: As targeted and immuno-therapies are increasingly adopted in the clinic, oncogenic mutations that were non-prognostic in the datasets analyzed may be able to predict sensitivity to specific therapeutic agents.
source: As targeted and immuno-therapies are increasingly adopted in the clinic, oncogenic mutations that were non-prognostic in the datasets analyzed here may be able to predict sensitivity to specific therapeutic agents (Gagan and Van Allen, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future clinical applications, supported by a citation.

claim: Tumors are composed of sub-clonal populations that harbor distinct sets of mutations, and cancer heterogeneity can influence clinical course.
source: Thirdly, tumors themselves are composed of sub-clonal populations that harbor distinct sets of mutations, and recent evidence suggests that cancer heterogeneity can influence clinical course (Jamal-Hanjani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jamal-Hanjani et al., 2017.

claim: Interrogating the mutational spectrum at the sub-clonal level may identify prognostic mutations not distinguished in bulk analyses.
source: Thus, interrogating the mutational spectrum at the sub-clonal level may identify prognostic mutations not distinguished in bulk analyses.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: Large-scale changes in tumor ploidy have previously been recognized as an indicator of poor outcome.
source: Though large-scale changes in tumor ploidy have previously been recognized as an indicator of poor outcome (Friedlander et al., 1984; Kallioniemi et al., 1987; Kokal et al., 1986; Merkel and McGuire, 1990; Zimmerman et al., 1987), the contributions of copy number alterations in most single genes have remained unexplored.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Despite the limited stratification value of mutations in cancer driver genes, copy number alterations of many of these same genes are broadly prognostic.
source: Despite the limited stratification value of mutations in cancer driver genes, we found that copy number alterations of many of these same genes are broadly prognostic.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: Focal CNAs tended to confer a worse prognosis than broad CNAs, consistent with a model in which large-scale gene dosage imbalances trigger proteotoxic stress and impose a fitness penalty on cancer cells.
source: Focal CNAs tended to confer a worse prognosis than broad CNAs, consistent with a model in which large-scale gene dosage imbalances trigger proteotoxic stress and impose a fitness penalty on cancer cells (Santaguida and Amon, 2015; Sheltzer and Amon, 2011).
evidence: This is stated directly in the discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Most CNAs remained prognostic whether or not they affected the expression of a mutated gene.
source: Moreover, while prognostic CNAs commonly caused proportional changes in target gene expression, most CNAs remained prognostic whether or not they affected the expression of a mutated gene.
evidence: This is stated directly in the discussion section.

claim: The study's results support a 'cancer gene island' or 'cumulative aneuploidy' model of tumorigenesis, in which cancers accumulate a series of limited copy number changes affecting haplo-sensitive and triplo-sensitive regions.
source: These results support a 'cancer gene island' or 'cumulative aneuploidy' model of tumorigenesis, in which cancers accumulate a series of limited copy number changes affecting haplo-sensitive and triplo-sensitive regions (Davoli et al., 2013; Solimini et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: Identifying the functional consequences of prognostic CNAs on tumor physiology is a key future goal.
source: Identifying the functional consequences of these prognostic CNAs on tumor physiology is a key future goal.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Many instances were discovered in which high-confidence biomarkers of aggressive disease also sensitized tumors to specific anti-cancer therapies.
source: We discovered many instances in which high-confidence biomarkers of aggressive disease also sensitized tumors to specific anti-cancer therapies.
evidence: This is stated directly in the discussion section.

claim: Several predicted sensitivities from the study have clinical or mechanistic support, including the use of CDK4/6 inhibitors to treat CDKN2A-deleted tumors, the use of PARP inhibitors to treat STAG2-mutant tumors, and the use of SYK inhibitors to treat RB1-mutant tumors.
source: Several predicted sensitivities from our work have clinical or mechanistic support, including the use of CDK4/6 inhibitors to treat CDKN2A-deleted tumors, the use of PARP inhibitors to treat STAG2-mutant tumors, and the use of SYK inhibitors to treat RB1-mutant tumors (Bailey et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2015b; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly in the discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Treatment with targeted agents significantly alters the cellular epigenetic and genetic landscape, often culminating in the development of resistance to the applied therapies.
source: Treatment with targeted agents significantly alters the cellular epigenetic and genetic landscape, often culminating in the development of resistance to the applied therapies (Holohan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Holohan et al., 2013.

claim: Secondary alterations that tumors evolve to tolerate targeted drugs could also alter or blunt the aggressive phenotype caused by the original driver alteration.
source: We speculate that secondary alterations that tumors evolve to tolerate these drugs could also alter or blunt the aggressive phenotype caused by the original driver alteration.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about tumor evolution.

claim: Targeting a biomarker that confers poor prognosis could both directly lead to improved patient outcomes by triggering a robust clinical response, and indirectly help patients by forcing tumor evolution away from dependence on a driver of aggressive disease.
source: In this way, targeting a biomarker that confers poor prognosis could both directly lead to improved patient outcomes by triggering a robust clinical response, and indirectly help patients by forcing tumor evolution away from dependence on a driver of aggressive disease.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential benefits of targeting prognostic biomarkers.

claim: For the TCGA genomic copy number analysis, the study used the HG19 segmented SCNAs, corrected for germline SCNAs.
source: For the TCGA genomic copy number analysis, we used the HG19 segmented SCNAs, corrected for germline SCNAs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section.

claim: Overall survival time was used as a clinical endpoint for all cancer types except PRAD.
source: Overall survival time was used as a clinical endpoint for all cancer types except PRAD.
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section.

claim: Overall survival was chosen because it reflects an objective and unambiguous event, it is the gold-standard for oncology clinical trials, and it is widely-available across different studies.
source: Overall survival was chosen because it reflects an objective and unambiguous event, it is the gold-standard for oncology clinical trials, and it is widely-available across different studies (Driscoll and Rixe, 2009).
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section and supported by a citation.

claim: For PRAD, 'days to biochemical recurrence' was used as a surrogate endpoint because fewer than 2% of the patients in the PRAD cohort died during the follow-up period.
source: However, as fewer than 2% of the patients in the PRAD cohort died during the follow-up period, 'days to biochemical recurrence' was used as a surrogate endpoint.
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section.

claim: Primary tumors (indicated with a '01' in the patient barcode) were used for every cancer type except SKCM.
source: Primary tumors (indicated with a '01' in the patient barcode) were used for every cancer type except SKCM; for this cancer, few primary samples were available, so metastatic samples (indicated with a '06' in the barcode) were included for patients in which no primary tumor was available.
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section.

claim: For SKCM, metastatic samples (indicated with a '06' in the barcode) were included for patients in which no primary tumor was available.
source: Primary tumors (indicated with a '01' in the patient barcode) were used for every cancer type except SKCM; for this cancer, few primary samples were available, so metastatic samples (indicated with a '06' in the barcode) were included for patients in which no primary tumor was available.
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section.

claim: Overall survival was used as a clinical endpoint for all ICGC cohorts except EOPC-DE.
source: Overall survival was used as a clinical endpoint for all cohorts except EOPC-DE; due to the few deaths in this cohort, recurrence-free survival was used as an endpoint.
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section.

claim: For EOPC-DE, recurrence-free survival was used as an endpoint due to the few deaths in this cohort.
source: Overall survival was used as a clinical endpoint for all cohorts except EOPC-DE; due to the few deaths in this cohort, recurrence-free survival was used as an endpoint.
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section.

claim: Cox proportional hazard analysis used the R survival package to compute Z scores and p values.
source: Cox proportional hazard analysis used the R survival package (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/survival/index.html) to compute Z scores and p values.
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section.

claim: Genes were only included in downstream analyses if they were mutated in 2% or more of the patients in a cancer type cohort.
source: For all analyses using TCGA mutation data, mutations annotated as silent were excluded. Genes were only included in downstream analyses if they were mutated in 2% or more of the patients in a cancer type cohort.
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section.

claim: Cox proportional hazards models are a threshold-independent method of performing survival analysis.
source: Note that Cox proportional hazards models are a threshold-independent method of performing survival analysis, and so no minimum or maximum threshold for a copy number alteration was specified.
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section.

claim: A tumor was defined as having a focal amplification or deletion if its copy number was greater than 0.3 or less than −0.3, and the chromosomal interval with a copy number greater than 80% of the copy number at the gene of interest was less than or equal to 3 Mb.
source: A tumor was defined as having a focal amplification or deletion if its copy number was greater than 0.3 or less than −0.3, and the chromosomal interval with a copy number greater than 80% of the copy number at the gene of interest was less than or equal to 3 Mb (Krijgsman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section and supported by a citation.

claim: Stouffer's method was used to combine Z scores from different cancer types.
source: This analysis created a single Z score for each gene by combining the per gene Z scores from each cancer type using Stouffer's method. To perform Stouffer's method, we took the sum of the Z scores for a single gene and divided that sum by the square root of the number of cancer types with Z scores for the gene (Stouffer, 1949).
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section and supported by a citation.

claim: A Benjamini-Hochberg correction with a 5% false-discovery rate was applied to the individual Z scores.
source: To account for greatly expanding the number of genes tested, we applied a Benjamini-Hochberg correction with a 5% false-discovery rate to the individual Z scores that we obtained.
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section.

claim: Code for the analysis is available on GitHub at https://github.com/joan-smith/genomic-features-survival.
source: Code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/joan-smith/genomic-features-survival (Smith, 2018; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/genomic-features-survival).
evidence: This is stated directly in the materials and methods section.

claim: Cox proportional hazards modeling was chosen because it does not require the selection of a threshold or cut-off for continuous data.
source: Cox proportional hazards modeling was chosen for several reasons. First, unlike Kaplan-Meier analysis, Cox models do not require the selection of a threshold or cut-off, so continuous data like gene expression values do not need to be dichotomized.
evidence: This is stated directly in Supplemental Text 1.

claim: Cox models can accept both continuous and discrete input data.
source: Secondly, Cox models can accept both continuous and discrete input data, allowing this approach to be used to analyze both binary (e.g., mutant vs. non-mutant) and continuous (e.g., gene copy number) genomic features.
evidence: This is stated directly in Supplemental Text 1.

claim: Cox models are amenable to both univariate and multivariate analyses.
source: Thirdly, Cox models are amenable to both univariate (i = 1) and multivariate (i > 1) analyses.
evidence: This is stated directly in Supplemental Text 1.

claim: Cox regression allows calculation of Z scores and a p value for each association.
source: Fourthly, Cox regression allows us to calculate Z scores and a p value for each association, as Z scores represent the number of standard deviations from the mean of a normal distribution.
evidence: This is stated directly in Supplemental Text 1.

claim: Z scores encode the directionality of an association: poor prognostic factors will exhibit βi values greater than 0, while favorable prognostic factors will exhibit βi values less than 0.
source: Fifthly, Z scores encode the directionality of an association: poor prognostic factors will exhibit βi values greater than 0, while favorable prognostic factors will exhibit βi values less than 0.
evidence: This is stated directly in Supplemental Text 1.

claim: Z scores are useful for meta-analyses, as they can be combined using Stouffer's Method.
source: Sixthly, Z scores are useful for meta-analyses, as they can be combined using Stouffer's Method (Stouffer, 1949):
evidence: This is stated directly in Supplemental Text 1 and supported by a citation.

claim: Cox proportional hazards modeling is commonly used in both previous genome-wide survival analyses and in numerous clinical biomarkers studies.
source: Seventhly, Cox proportional hazards modeling is commonly used in both previous genome-wide survival analyses and in numerous clinical biomarkers studies (Dhanasekaran et al., 2001; Fukuoka et al., 2011; Gentles et al., 2015; Parker et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2005), facilitating comparison with other biomarker discovery efforts.
evidence: This is stated directly in Supplemental Text 1 and supported by multiple citations.

claim: A 2% threshold was selected to balance between maintaining the normality of the Z score distribution while also retaining infrequent but significant mutations in driver genes.
